title: Renormalization Group Flow Matching for Scalable Local Generative Modeling
abstract: Despite their remarkable success in modeling complex data, generative models face a fundamental tradeoff. Global approaches can capture full structural coherence but suffer from high computational costs, while local models are efficient but often fail to reproduce long-range correlations and global coherence. The renormalization group (RG) bridges this gap by seamlessly connecting spatial structures across different length scales, retaining quasi-local descriptions at each step while preserving long-range correlations. We introduce renormalization group flow matching (RGFM), a generative framework that systematically structures data generation across different spatial scales. By using an exact RG flow as the probability path, RGFM progressively generates data from long- to short-wavelength structures. To reconcile scalability with global structure, we exploit two key properties of the RG: quasi-locality and scale separation. We rigorously show that the RGFM probability flow can be accurately approximated by local velocity fields acting over a spatial range $O(Λ^{-1}[\ln L+\ln(1/\varepsilon)])$ for RG wavenumber scale $Λ$, linear system size $L$, and prescribed error tolerance $\varepsilon$. This property enables local generative modeling with patches of size $O(\ln L)$ and a computational cost that scales nearly linearly with the system volume. We numerically demonstrate that local RGFM reproduces long-range correlations far beyond its receptive field in representative one-dimensional distributions, while conventional local flow matching exhibits substantial errors at long distances. On FFHQ images, RGFM yields far more coherent and higher-quality samples than local flow matching at 64x64 and 256x256. Our results establish RG-guided probability flows as a promising route toward scalable generative modeling that captures long-range structure using only local computation.
summary: This work introduces Renormalization Group Flow Matching (RGFM), a novel generative model that overcomes the scalability limitations of global models and the correlation deficiencies of purely local models. By embedding the systematic scale-connecting mechanism of the Renormalization Group into the flow matching process, RGFM enables the generation of highly coherent, long-range structured data using only local computations. This establishes RG-guided flows as a powerful paradigm for scalable generative modeling.
main_problem: Generative models face a tradeoff between the global coherence of expensive global methods and the efficiency but limited long-range correlation of local models.
main_result: The proposed Renormalization Group Flow Matching (RGFM) framework successfully generates high-quality samples that capture long-range correlations using only local computations.
method: RGFM integrates the exact Renormalization Group (RG) flow as the probability path within a flow matching framework, progressively generating data from long- to short-wavelength structures.
model_or_system: The model is a generative framework applied to complex, high-dimensional data (like images or physical field configurations), utilizing the mathematical structure of the RG to guide the probability flow.
key_observables: Global coherence, long-range correlations, and sample quality (e.g., FID score on FFHQ images).
important_parameters: RG wavenumber scale (Λ), system size (L), and error tolerance (ε).
main_assumptions: The RGFM probability flow can be accurately approximated by local velocity fields acting over a specific, calculable spatial range derived from the RG structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of local generative modeling, the RGFM probability path involving RG diffusion and site-decimation, and direct comparisons showing RGFM's superior global coherence over standard local flow matching for images.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the fundamental tradeoff in generative modeling, introduces RGFM by leveraging the RG's ability to connect scales, provides a theoretical analysis proving the locality of the flow approximation, and validates the method numerically on 1D and 2D image data.
why_interesting: The paper bridges the mathematical tools of RG theory, traditionally used for critical phenomena, directly into the computational framework of modern generative AI, providing a physically motivated mechanism for achieving scalability while preserving global structure.
